harder.updated_question: what animal tests for endocrine disruption were done in the past? are they still done?
harder.verification_criterion: The answer identifies at least three specific historical animal test methods/assays used for endocrine disruption testing (e.g., uterotrophic assay, Hershberger assay, fish vitellogenin assay) with their approximate time periods of use.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of animal testing for endocrine disruption (ED), what has been done historically, how use has evolved, where it is still conducted today, and current trends toward replacement.

Summary
Historically, endocrine disruption testing relied on tiered in vivo batteries across mammals, fish, and amphibians to probe estrogen, androgen, thyroid, and steroidogenic modes of action, with U.S. EPA OPPTS and OECD guidelines formalizing these assays for regulatory use. Over the past decade, jurisdictions (notably the EU and UK) have substantially reduced animal testing for cosmetics and have increasingly embraced OECD-aligned in vitro/in silico methods and weight-of-evidence approaches for endocrine endpoints; however, animal testing remains required or used in pesticide/bicide assessments and for certain rodent reproductive/thyroid screens where regulatory frameworks still demand conclusive adversity evidence. <cite id="73028920-0">Fish-focused OECD TGs (229, 230, 234, 240) and rodent OECD TGs (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) cover estrogen/androgen/steroidogenesis modalities, with amphibian TGs (231, 241, 248) for thyroid disruption; fish assays have become the primary non-mammalian vertebrate approach in environmental ED assessment</cite><cite id="73028920-1">Amphibian metamorphosis assay (OECD TG 231), larval growth/development (241), and Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid assay (248) are standardized in vivo options for thyroid-related endocrine disruption, whereas mammalian ED assessment relies on rodent assays such as TGs 407, 408, 416, 421, 422, and 443</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-2">OECD Guidance Document 150 and OPPTS guidelines provide a conceptual framework and standardized test descriptions for EATS pathways and are the basis for international data acceptance in regulatory assessments of endocrine disruption</cite>.

What animal tests have been done (historical and cross-jurisdiction)
Mammalian in vivo batteries (rodent reproductive and thyroid screens)
- In the U.S., the EPA Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) historically used four in vivo rodent assays spanning estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways: Female Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function (OPPTS 890.1450) and Male Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function (OPPTS 890.1500), with endpoint suites including vaginal opening, estrous cyclicity, tissue weights, serum hormones (thyroxine, TSH), and histopathology; these assays were designed to detect disruption of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal and thyroid axes in rats, and are part of the legacy OPPTS framework that informed OECD test design and acceptance. <cite id="3e35f408-1">The EDSP includes four in vivo mammalian assays screening estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways via rat pubertal development and thyroid function endpoints, with performance criteria demonstrably attainable and repeatable across labs</cite>.
- Estrogen/androgen receptor uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style screens and related rodent assays (e.g., OECD TG 443 rat uterotrophic assay; OECD TG 416 for androgen receptor activity in males) have long been used, often paired with fish-based vitellogenin screens to increase throughput while preserving biological plausibility. <cite id="3e35f408-0">The OECD 440 uterotrophic assay is used by the U.S. EPA EDSP; tiered approaches have combined in vitro receptor screening with fish vitellogenin assays to detect estrogen-sensitive endocrine effects</cite><cite id="3e35f408-3">The uterotrophic assay was developed under EPA EDSP (OCSPP 890.1600) and used in adult or immature rodent formats to detect estrogen-sensitive uterine responses</cite>.
- Steroidogenesis assays using H295R human adrenal cells are now widely recognized by OECD (TG 456) and EPA EDSP as Level 2 in vitro screens to detect perturbation of estrogen and testosterone production, and are integrated within OECD 150’s stepwise framework to reduce or replace animal testing when sufficient mechanistic and WOE data are available. <cite id="3e35f408-2">OECD TG 456 and EPA EDSP guideline 890.1550 recognize the H295R steroidogenesis assay; OECD 150 identifies Level 2 in vitro assays, including H295R, as mechanistic tools to determine endocrine activity and prioritize further testing</cite>.

Non-mammalian vertebrate in vivo assays (fish and amphibian)
- Fish assays historically and currently serve as core ED screening and tiered endpoints for environmental chemicals. OECD TG 229 (short-term fish reproduction), TG 230 (21-day fish screening), TG 234 (fish sexual development), and TG 240 (Medaka extended one-generation reproduction) provide standardized designs to detect estrogen-, androgen-, steroidogenesis-related, and thyroid-related disruption in fish, with increasing inclusion of thyroid endpoints in recent years. <cite id="73028920-0">OECD TGs 229, 230, 234, and 240 cover estrogen/androgen/steroidogenesis endpoints in fish; zebrafish has been widely used in in vivo ED studies, though thyroid-specific guidance historically lagged</cite>.
- Amphibian assays (metamorphosis, larval growth/development, and Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid) are standardized OECD TGs (231, 241, 248) and are recommended for thyroid-mode investigations in non-mammalian taxa, offering higher-tier biological relevance when exposure warrants. <cite id="73028920-1">Standardized amphibian assays (231, 241, 248) are recommended for investigating endocrine activity via the thyroid modality in non-mammalian vertebrates due to the amphibian TH axis control of metamorphosis</cite>.
- In pesticide/biocide contexts, EU/EFSA/ECHA frameworks have promoted tiered fish assays for ecological hazard identification and recommended amphibian assays for thyroid modes when needed; this reflects a shift toward aquatic vertebrates for environmental ED screening while retaining rodent assays for human-relevant endpoints. <cite id="73028920-0">EU projects have optimized aquatic vertebrate tests and moved to include thyroid endpoints in fish guidelines to reduce reliance on amphibians, with EATS modalities covered across TGs</cite><cite id="73028920-3">OECD’s conceptual framework and Level 3–5 tests (e.g., TG 229, 230, 231) are used in EU data requirements for PPP; EFSA’s tiered guidance emphasizes in vivo mammalian and fish assays for diverse hormonal functions, with amphibians prioritized at higher tiers if exposure concerns arise</cite><cite id="73028920-4">A tiered approach integrating exposure with hazard characterization recommends in vivo mammalian and fish assays for screening across estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways, with amphibians considered at higher tiers depending on exposure; avian and invertebrate tests can follow for reproductive and endocrine-mediated effects</cite>.

Cosmetics sector: large-scale decline and replacement
- The EU phased in a full ban on animal testing and sale of animal-tested cosmetics between 2004 (finished products) and 2009–2013 (ingredients), precipitating major reductions in cosmetic mammalian ED testing and parallel adoption of OECD in vitro methods for skin/eye irritation and acceptance of alternatives; similar bans or phase-outs have since been adopted in the UK, Turkey, Taiwan, New Zealand, and others. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">The UK first banned cosmetic animal testing in 1998; the EU implemented phased bans culminating in 2013, following which India adopted a 2014 ban and accepted OECD in vitro skin and eye irritation methods</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU legislation adopted scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors in 2017, effective for PPP/biocides in 2018, reinforcing a shift to alternative models and ethical strategies for endocrine assessment</cite>.
- EU-wide counts show mammalian ingredient testing peaked at 5,571 animals in 2005 and dropped to 1,245 by 2008, with the decline attributed to the ban’s first stages; these counts explicitly exclude ecotoxicity (fish LC50), reflecting regulatory movement away from mammalian toxicity for cosmetics. <cite id="bc9ecaed-4">Between 2004 and 2009 EU data show 5,571 mammalian toxicity animals in 2005 and 1,245 in 2008 for cosmetic ingredients, after the EU banned finished product testing in 2004 and ingredient testing phases in 2009; the full ban was completed in 2013</cite>.

How regulatory frameworks evolved and what they require now
- OECD Guidance Document 150 and OPPTS guidelines formalize a Conceptual Framework (levels 1–5) across biological organization to evaluate endocrine activity/adversity and to integrate in vitro, in silico, and in vivo evidence; this framework underpins mutual acceptance of data and has been adopted by EU biocide and PPP regulations. <cite id="bc9ecaed-2">OECD 150 provides guidance on interpreting test outcomes, tabulating endpoints and affected pathways, and using a Conceptual Framework for Testing and Assessment of Endocrine Disruptors to organize methods and determine additional testing needs; OECD/OPPTS methods are the basis for data acceptance in regulatory assessments</cite>.
- In the EU and ECHA/EFSA guidance for pesticides, in vivo fish assays (TG 229, 230, 234, 240) are primary for environmental ED screening, with amphibian assays recommended for thyroid modes and mammalian rodent assays still used for human-relevant endocrine adversity; integrated approaches and Level 2 in vitro assays (e.g., H295R, yeast estrogen screens) are encouraged to reduce animal use where sufficient evidence exists. <cite id="73028920-0">Testing across EATS modalities is covered by standardized TGs; fish have become the prime vertebrate class for ED assessment in the environment</cite><cite id="73028920-1">Amphibian assays (231, 241, 248) are recommended for thyroid-related ED investigation in non-mammalian species; rodent assays (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) underpin human assessment</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R steroidogenesis assays (OECD 456; EPA 890.1550) are recognized Level 2 in vitro methods that inform endocrine activity and prioritize further testing</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU data requirements have historically not been designed specifically for ED identification; OECD framework-level 3–5 tests (e.g., TG 229, 230, 231) are now included, with fish and amphibian assays prioritized for screening and higher-tier characterization</cite>.
- The EU has moved to adopt scientific criteria for endocrine disruption (effective for PPPs in 2018) and has incorporated OECD acceptance of in vitro test methods and Good In Vitro Method Practices, signaling a regulatory preference for integrated approaches that can de-incriminate or avoid animal tests when robust mechanistic and exposure evidence is available. <cite id="bc9ecaed-1">Scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors adopted by the EU in 2017/2018 align with WHO definitions and require datasets to assess disruptive capacity, encouraging alternative models when animal testing is not necessary</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD published guidance on defined approaches and accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes, and developed Good In Vitro Method Practices to extend GLP to in vitro methods</cite>.

Are these tests still being done today?
- Cosmetics and personal care: Following the EU’s completed ban (2013) and UK’s earlier ban (1998), and subsequent bans/phase-outs in multiple countries, animal testing for endocrine endpoints in cosmetics has been substantially reduced or eliminated; however, animal use persisted for ingredient testing until the phased implementation and is now being replaced by OECD-accepted in vitro methods in OECD-aligned jurisdictions. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">UK (1998) and EU (2013) bans led to adoption of OECD in vitro irritation/corrosion methods and harmonization of bans in India (2014)</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-4">EU ingredient mammalian testing fell from 5,571 in 2005 to 1,245 in 2008 before and during the first stage of the ban (2009), with the full ban completed by 2013</cite>.
- Plant protection products and biocides: EU and other regulators still require in vivo fish and amphibian assays for ED screening and characterization in environmental risk assessments; rodent assays remain the reference for human-relevant endocrine adversity, and Level 2 in vitro assays are increasingly requested to reduce animal numbers while providing mechanistic evidence. <cite id="73028920-0">EU projects optimize aquatic vertebrate tests and include thyroid endpoints in fish TGs to reduce amphibian reliance; fish assays (TG 229, 230, 234, 240) are central for ED identification in the environment</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide data requirements now incorporate OECD framework tests (229, 230, 231), with fish and amphibian assays prioritized for screening and higher-tier characterization</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">Regulatory agencies regularly request Level 2 in vitro assays (e.g., H295R) to determine endocrine activity of PPPs under OECD 150</cite>.
- Human health endpoints in general chemicals: U.S. EPA EDSP continues to use in vivo rodent assays for conclusive adversity assessment, alongside tiered in vitro approaches; OECD TGs (e.g., 440/443) and OPPTS protocols remain in use, but agencies increasingly accept Tox21-style in vitro/IT strategies to waive some animal tests when evidence is sufficient. <cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s in vivo rodent assays for estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways (e.g., OPPTS 890.1450/1500) remain standardized</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA’s collaboration with Tox21 enabled waivers of animal-based uterotrophic testing, marking the first regulatory use of this approach to replace animal testing</cite>.
- Research and surveillance: Scientists continue to run classic rodent uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style and fish vitellogenin assays to detect estrogenicity in emerging compounds (e.g., PFAS), reflecting ongoing use of established assays even as alternatives proliferate. <cite id="3e35f408-0">PFAS have been screened for estrogen receptor activation and endocrine disruption using uterotrophic assays (OECD 440/EDSP), with tiered strategies pairing in vitro receptor screening and fish vitellogenin assays</cite><cite id="3e35f408-3">Adult and immature rat uterotrophic formats detect estrogen-sensitive uterine responses and remain a standard in regulatory-guided screening</cite>.

What has replaced animal tests and how accepted are alternatives?
- In vitro mechanistic assays and integrated approaches: The H295R steroidogenesis assay (OECD 456; EPA 890.1550), yeast estrogen screen (YES), and other Level 2 methods are recognized by OECD/EPA to detect pathway-level disruption and reduce or replace animal testing when combined with computational models and weight-of-evidence reasoning. <cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R steroidogenesis assays are recognized by OECD and EPA to detect perturbation of estrogen and testosterone production and are used within OECD 150 to prioritize additional testing or conclude endocrine activity</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">Alternative models are required to assess endocrine safety for cosmetics ethically; OECD 150 describes how adversity can be assessed using validated in vitro/embryonic models to cover EATS pathways without animal experimentation when justified</cite>.
- Institutional acceptance and Good Practice: OECD has accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes and formalized Good In Vitro Method Practices (GIVIMP), enabling broader acceptance of in vitro ED assays in regulatory dossiers. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes and published Good In Vitro Method Practices to extend GLP to in vitro methods</cite>.
- Weight-of-evidence and regulatory WOs: Multiple jurisdictions now implement integrated approaches to testing and assessment (IATA), encouraging combinations of defined approaches (e.g., in vitro receptor assays, H295R, QSAR) to de-incriminate or avoid animal tests when data gaps are small and exposure is low; EU legislation explicitly adopts scientific criteria to define ED properties and aligns with OECD frameworks. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD published guidance on defined approaches and reporting within integrated testing strategies</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU adopted scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors in 2017/2018 aligned with WHO definitions and supports the use of alternative models and ethical strategies for endocrine assessment</cite>.

Putting it together: historical practices and current status
- What was done: Endocrine disruption testing historically relied on in vivo mammalian rodent reproductive/developmental assays (estrogen, androgen, thyroid) and non-mammalian vertebrate assays in fish and amphibians to probe EATS modalities; these were standardized by U.S. OPPTS and OECD and implemented across pesticides, biocides, and cosmetics. <cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s rodent pubertal and thyroid function assays provided standardized screens for hormonal disruption</cite><cite id="73028920-0">OECD TGs 229, 230, 234, and 240 cover fish EATS endpoints; amphibian TGs (231, 241, 248) target thyroid disruption; rodent TGs (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) underpin human assessment</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide guidance incorporated OECD framework and fish/amphibian assays to identify ED properties in non-target organisms</cite>.
- Are they still done? Today, in vivo ED assays remain required or frequently used for environmental hazard identification (fish and amphibian assays) and for human-relevant adversity in regulatory frameworks, especially for PPPs and biocides; rodent uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style and other in vivo assays are still run by EPA and researchers, but OECD/EPA frameworks now enable waivers or replacement in many cases via Tox21-style strategies and recognized in vitro assays. <cite id="73028920-0">Fish assays are the prime vertebrate class for ED assessment in the environment, with amphibians covering thyroid modes</cite><cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP continues to use four in vivo rodent assays for mammalian ED screening</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA’s Tox21 collaboration enabled waivers of animal uterotrophic testing, marking the first regulatory use of this approach</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD accepted fish cell-line ecotoxicity tests and established GIVIMP, supporting broader acceptance of in vitro methods</cite>.
- Sectoral trends: Cosmetics testing in OECD-aligned jurisdictions has been largely halted or replaced by in vitro methods following EU/UK bans, with counts of mammalian ingredient tests dropping precipitously in the EU before and after the phased ban; in contrast, pesticide/biocide and broader chemical safety assessments still rely on in vivo assays but increasingly integrate OECD-accepted in vitro tools and weight-of-evidence to minimize animal use. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">EU/UK bans and adoption of OECD in vitro methods catalyzed large-scale replacement of cosmetic animal tests</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-4">EU ingredient mammalian testing fell from 5,571 to 1,245 animals between 2005 and 2008 as the first stage of the ban took effect (full ban by 2013)</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide guidance incorporates OECD TGs for fish and amphibian assays and emphasizes integrated approaches</cite>.

What to expect next
Regulators and industry are moving toward routine use of defined approaches and integrated testing strategies, with OECD and EFSA/ECHA explicitly endorsing in vitro, in silico, and GLP-extended methods; this trajectory implies further reductions in animal testing for endocrine endpoints where mechanistic and exposure data are strong, with in vivo studies reserved for cases requiring conclusive adversity evidence or where alternatives are insufficient. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD’s defined approaches reporting guidance and acceptance of fish cell-line ecotoxicity tests, along with GIVIMP, support broader adoption of in vitro methods</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU criteria define endocrine disruption via mode of action, adverse effect, and plausibility, encouraging datasets that leverage in vitro/embryonic models to avoid animal experimentation when feasible</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">Recognition of H295R and other Level 2 assays within OECD 150 enables regulatory determinations of endocrine activity and prioritization of additional testing, reducing reliance on animals where evidence suffices</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- Yes, many of the classic in vivo animal tests for endocrine disruption have long been used and are still used in certain jurisdictions and sectors—especially for environmental hazard identification (fish, amphibian) and human-relevant adversity (rodent reproductive/thyroid screens). <cite id="73028920-0">Fish and amphibian assays remain core to environmental ED testing, with rodent assays for human adversity</cite><cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s rodent assays continue as standardized screens</cite>.
- No, they are not universally “still” required: OECD/EU/US frameworks increasingly accept and mandate the use of in vitro, in silico, and integrated approaches to replace or reduce animal testing for endocrine endpoints, with cosmetics largely off the animal-testing track in many jurisdictions and tiered strategies (e.g., Tox21) enabling waivers in some mammalian assays. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA has used Tox21 to waive animal uterotrophic tests; OECD accepts fish cell-line ecotoxicity and formalizes GIVIMP</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU criteria and OECD 150 encourage alternative models and integrated approaches to avoid animal testing when sufficient evidence exists</cite>.
- What to watch: Continued OECD/EU acceptance of in vitro ED assays (e.g., H295R, yeast estrogen screens) and growth of integrated approaches will likely further de-incriminate animal tests for endocrine disruption in human health risk assessments, while in vivo fish/amphibian assays will remain pivotal for environmental risk characterization where full biological and exposure context is required. <cite id="73028920-0">EU efforts to include thyroid endpoints in fish TGs aim to reduce amphibian reliance while covering EATS modalities in non-mammalian vertebrates</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R and other Level 2 assays provide mechanistic evidence and support regulatory decisions to minimize animal testing</cite>.

Title: Development of the integrated fish endocrine disruptor test—Part B: Implementation of thyroid‐related endpoints
Snippet: Various ongoing European Union (EU) research projects are working on the optimization of aquatic vertebrate tests for the identification of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs; Holbech et al., 2020).Attempts are being made to cover as many relevant modes of action as possible, to include thyroid-related endpoints in existing fish test guidelines (TGs) and thus, to reduce existing amphibian tests.Testing for the different endocrine modalities (EATS: estrogen, androgen, thyroid, and steroidogenesis) is covered in different TGs for nontarget organisms (ECHA/EFSA, 2018).For nonmammalian vertebrates, tests covering endpoints for estrogen-, androgen-, and steroidogenesis-related effects in fish are covered by TGs 229 (Fish Short-Term Reproduction Assay [FSTRA]; OECD, 2012), 230 (21-Day Fish Assay;OECD, 2009b), 234 (Fish Sexual Development Test [FSDT]; OECD, 2011), and 240 (Medaka Extended One Generation Reproduction Test; OECD, 2023).Fish have thus become the prime vertebrate class for the assessment of EDCs in the environment.

However, although zebrafish (Danio rerio) has been the major nonmammalian model utilized in studies evaluating in vivo effects on the TH system or discussing regulatory concerns over the past five years (Couderq et al., 2020), none of these TGs addresses potential TH system disruption (THSD).So far, in an environmental context, thyroid-related endocrine disruption is covered only for amphibians by three OECD TGs (TGs 231, 241, and 248;OECD, 2009a), and assessment of THSD for humans is based mainly on rodent assays such as TGs 407, 408, 416, 421, 422, and 443 (ECHA/EFSA, 2018).
</snippet>

Title: Amphibian studies to investigate the endocrine-disrupting properties of chemicals through the thyroid modality: a comparison of their statistical power
Snippet: Regulation 2018/605 (European Commission, 2018) lays down the scientific criteria for the identification of pesticide active substances having endocrine-disrupting (ED) properties. To support the implementation of those criteria, a guidance document was jointly developed by the European Chemical Agency (ECHA) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) with the participation of the Joint Research Centre (ECHA/EFSA, 2018). In accordance with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) guidance document on standardised test guidelines for evaluating chemicals for endocrine disruption (OECD, 2018), the ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends using amphibian studies for investigating the ED properties in nonmammalian species through the Thyroid-(T) modality, because it is well established that amphibian metamorphosis is under the control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. In case of uncertainties around some of the definitions used in this study, for example, "endocrine activity," "endocrine adversity," "sufficiently investigate," "T-modality," "T-mediated," "positive findings," "screening assay," and so forth, please refer to the ECHA/EFSA Guidance (2018) for clarification. Two standardized in vivo amphibian study designs are available to sufficiently investigate the endocrine activity and/or adversity of plant protection products through the T-modality. These studies are the amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA, OECD test guideline 231, OECD, 2009; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency [USEPA], 2009) and the larval amphibian growth and developmental assay (LADGA, OECD test guideline 241, OECD, 2015;USEPA, 2015). A third assay, the Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid assay (XETA, OECD test guideline 248, OECD, 2019) is also available. However, the XETA is only aimed at detecting thyroid active compounds based on induction of fluorescence compared to controls (Arena & van der Linden, 2021).
</snippet>

Title: Computational Approaches to Chemical Hazard Assessment
Snippet: The OECD guideline identifier provides detailed descriptions of different experimental procedures. OECD TG 407, for example, is the OECD guideline for the test "Repeated Dose 28-Day Oral Toxicity Study in Rodents" (OECD, 2008). This is a 13-page guideline, which has a revision history (one major change in 1995) that covers important initial considerations, the principle of the test, and a detailed description of the method. These guidelines describe in some detail how to interpret the results of guideline studies and what parameters may be changed for the study. Parameter choices for TG 407 include selection of animal species (preferably rats, but any rodent with sufficient justification.) The ability to change parameter selection for guidelines allows greater experimental variance. OECD guideline outcomes make excellent QSAR targets. They are the result of a well-defined study with careful instructions on how to measure the results. However, even using results from OECD guidelines studies is not without peril. In a study of the consistency of the Draize rabbit eye irritation test (another OECD guideline study), we found a low rate of concordance between studies (Luechtefeld et al., 2016b). Variance in repeated guideline study results can be large and bias can exist between labs performing experiments.

Title: Guidance on tiered risk assessment for plant protection products for aquatic organisms in edge-of-field surface waters
Snippet: As set out in Annex II, Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 makes specific provision only to approve an a.s., safener or synergist ‗if it is not considered to have endocrine disrupting properties that may cause adverse effects on non-target organisms unless the exposure […] is negligible' (section 3.8.2). It follows from this wording that the regulation takes a hazard-based approach to approval where endocrine disrupters are concerned.

Test methods currently required in the data requirement for environmental effects in the PPP Regulation are not designed specifically for identification of endocrine disrupters. However the OECD conceptual framework for testing and assessment of potential endocrine disrupters (OECD, 2012a) includes several test guidelines (in levels 3, 4 and 5) designed for identification of endocrine disrupting properties relevant to wildlife. Of relevance to the current Guidance on aquatic toxicity, these include the fish short-term reproduction assay (OECD TG 229), the 21-day fish screening assay (OECD TG 230), the amphibian metamorphosis assay (OECD TG 231), and the androgenised female stickleback screen (GD 140) at level 3 (in vivo tests providing data about selected endocrine mechanisms/pathways), the fish sexual development test at level 4 (in vivo assays providing data on adverse effects on endocrine-relevant endpoints), and the fish full life cycle ( Robust scientific criteria for identification of substances with ‗endocrine disrupting properties' are therefore needed to inform updated data requirements in support of this provision of the regulation, and by 14 December 2013 the Commission must present a draft proposal for such criteria. Pending these criteria, substances identified under Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 (classification and labelling) as C2 and R2, or R2 with evidence of toxicity to endocrine organs, shall be considered to have endocrine disrupting properties, with respect to human health assessment. There is currently no provision for identifying endocrine disruptors within the environmental effects assessment required for the regulation.

Title: Ecological risk assessment of endocrine disruptors.
Snippet: The European Centre for Ecotoxicology and Toxicology of Chemicals proposes a tiered approach for the ecological risk assessment of endocrine disruptors, integrating exposure and hazard (effects) characterization. Exposure assessment for endocrine disruptors should direct specific tests for wildlife species, placing hazard data into a risk assessment context. Supplementing the suite of mammalian screens now under Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) validation, high priority should be given to developing a fish screening assay for detecting endocrine activity in oviparous species. Taking into account both exposure characterization and alerts from endocrine screening, higher tier tests are also a priority for defining adverse effects. We propose that in vivo mammalian and fish assays provide a comprehensive screening battery for diverse hormonal functions (including androgen, estrogen, and thyroid hormone), whereas Amphibia should be considered at higher tiers if there are exposure concerns. Higher tier endocrine-disruptor testing should include fish development and fish reproduction tests, whereas a full life-cycle test could be subsequently used to refine aquatic risk assessments when necessary. For avian risk assessment, the new OECD Japanese quail reproduction test guideline provides a valuable basis for developing a test to detecting endocrine-mediated reproductive effects; this species could be used, where necessary, for an avian life-cycle test. For aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, data from existing developmental and reproductive tests remain of high value for ecological risk assessment. High priority should be given to research into comparative endocrine physiology of invertebrates to support data extrapolation to this diverse fauna.

Title: 60 Years of the 3Rs Symposium: Lessons Learned and the Road Ahead
Snippet: • South Korea passes a law to partially ban the manufacture and sale of animal-tested cosmetic products and ingredients if government-recognized, non-animal alternatives exist. 

• Russia introduces a bill to phase out the production and sale of animal-tested cosmetics and cosmetic ingredients if validated alternatives exist. 

• Turkey bans cosmetic animal testing and the sale of animal-tested cosmetic products and ingredients where a validated alternative exists. 

• New Zealand bans cosmetic animal testing for finished products and ingredients intended exclusively for use in cosmetics.

Title: Safety Testing of Cosmetic Products: Overview of Established Methods and New Approach Methodologies (NAMs)
Snippet: On the 13 December 2017 the European Parliament adopted scientific criteria to define endocrine disruptors which came into force for plant protection products and biocides in 2018 [72]. This has been a major step towards the future implementation of similar criteria for regulation of cosmetics in Europe. Despite the discrepancies due to the particular context of cosmetics, a few lessons relating to endocrine assessment strategies have been learnt from experience. 

Adopted criteria for endocrine disruptors are closely related to the WHO definition of 2012 [73]. An endocrine disruptor is defined by three main criteria: its endocrine mode of action, its capacity to cause an adverse effect, and the plausible link between this endocrine activity and the related adverse outcome. 

Regulatory authorities require datasets to permit a conclusive assessment on the disruptive capacity of an endocrine active sample. However, for cosmetic ingredients this will be difficult as availability of comprehensive endocrine test systems is very limited without accessing animal experimentation. Therefore, alternative models will be required to overcome this difficulty that can provide data which will contribute to safety of cosmetics for the endocrine system in an ethical manner. 

Since 2002, experts representing OECD member countries have published test guidelines dedicated to endocrine assessment of chemicals. These internationally acknowledged methods are listed, and their proper usage is described within the OECD Guidance Document 150 [74]. According to this document, adversity should be assessed (using laboratory animals) to achieve a conclusive assessment of an endocrine disruptor. OECD validated methods cover so far EATS (Estrogen, Androgen, Thyroid, and Steroidogenic) endocrine pathways, for which specific adverse physiological outcomes have been characterized. 

It could be argued that the absence of endocrine activity excludes the need for investigating physiological adversity. This opens a possible testing strategy for an ethical cosmetic approach: using a battery of validated in vitro/embryonic models to cover all major modes of action of endocrine disruptors on EATS pathways.
</snippet>

Title: Advancing Endocrine Disruptors via In Vitro Evaluation: Recognizing the Significance of the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development and United States Environmental Protection Agency Guidelines, Embracing New Assessment Methods, and the Urgent Need for a Comprehensive Battery of Tests
Snippet: The OECD (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development) is an intergovernmental organization in which representatives of 38 industrialized countries in North and South America, Europe, and the Asia and Pacific region, as well as the European Commission, meet to coordinate and harmonize policies, discuss issues of mutual concern, and work together to respond to international problems. The OECD has developed a number of test guidelines and methods for the testing and assessment of chemical substances. The OECD guidance document 150 on standardized test guidelines for evaluating chemicals for endocrine disruption is intended to provide guidance for interpreting the outcome of individual tests and compiling evidence on whether or not a substance may be an endocrine disruptor [25]. The guidance document also provides a general description of each standardized test guideline and tabular presentations of the endpoints measured in each test and the endocrine pathway affected. The document also describes a Conceptual Framework for Testing and Assessment of Endocrine Disruptors that helps organize available test methods at different levels of biological organization to determine additional testing needs or conclude about the potential endocrine disruptor action of a chemical. The OECD guidelines and methods serve as a basis for mutual acceptance of data so that they are widely used by regulatory authorities and industry to assess the safety of chemicals. For example, the guidance for the identification of endocrine disruptors in the context of Regulations (EU) No 528/2012 concerning the making available on the market and use of biocidal products [26] and (EC) No 1107/2009 concerning the placing of plant protection products on the market [27] refers to the OECD guidelines (European Chemical Agency (ECHA) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) with the technical support of the Joint Research Centre [28]. 

The OPPTS (Office of Pollution Prevention and Toxics) is a division within the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that is responsible for developing and implementing policies, programs, and regulations related to pollution prevention and chemical management. The OPPTS has developed a number of guidelines that provide recommendations and guidance for conducting various types of environmental testing and risk assessment. The EPA OPPTS guidelines are developed specifically for use in the United States, and they are primarily focused on regulatory compliance under US law.
</snippet>

Title: Cosmetic Regulation and Alternatives to Animal Experimentation in India
Snippet: United Kingdom was the first to ban animal testing of cosmetics, and it happened in 1998. The European Union (EU) went through legislations and endeavors implementing animal testing ban in a phased manner, and the final step was done in 2013. Consequent to this, there was enormous canvassing for ban of cosmetic testing on animals in India, to harmonize the marketing as well as import ban of EU. The Indian Drug and Cosmetic Regulatory Authority conceded the demand resulting in the final ban in 2014. This review traces the evolution of thought sequence resulting in the ban, and approval of adopting OECD Guidelines for in vitro testing of skin and eye irritation and corrosion.

Title: Safety evaluations under the proposed US Safe Cosmetics and Personal Care Products Act of 2013: animal use and cost estimates.
Snippet: Under US law, laboratories that use animals for testing are inspected by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the USDA inspection reports include the number of animals; however, the reports exclude mice and rats, and they do not break out the number of animals by testing purpose (for example, for cosmetics testing). The USDA reports, therefore, cannot provide supporting information for this estimate of cosmetics testing. 

The European Union, however, does include mice and rats in reports and does break out animals by testing purpose. Table 8 summarizes the EU reports for 2005 and 2008, which were the last two reports before the first stage of the EU's ban on animal testing for cosmetic ingredients took effect in 2009 (the full ban was completed in 2013). We can know these tests were for ingredients, rather than for finished cosmetics, because the EU banned animal testing of finished cosmetic products in 2004, so all cosmetic-related animal tests between 2004 and 2009 can only be for ingredients. The total number of animals for mammalian toxicity tests in the 2005 EU report is 5,571, and in the 2008 EU report is 1,245 (EC, 2007(EC, , 2010)). Note that the 2008 report lists a total of 1,967 animals, but 722 are fish, presumably for the LC50 fish toxicity test. Since we are not considering ecotoxicity tests in this article, the 722 fish are excluded here, resulting in the total of 1,245. 

Much of the difference between the 2005 and 2008 totals likely relates to more ingredients having been tested in 2005. Also, in 2005, some ingredients underwent repeated dose tests, whereas the ingredients in 2008 did not. Such year to year differences are expected: Since relatively few ingredients fall into adverse effects on the development of humans or animals, including effects on the female or male reproductive system, the endocrine system, fertility, pregnancy, pregnancy outcomes, or modifications in other functions of the body that are dependent on the integrity of the reproductive system as well normal fetal development" (section 611 [10]). 

The Act clearly identifies a requirement to determine, for each ingredient, an exposure scenario that will "produce no adverse health effects."

Title: PFAS Modulate Osmotic Signaling Independent of Gravimetric Changes in the Rat Uterus
Snippet: Per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a large class of fluorinated organic chemicals that are ubiquitous and persistent in humans and the environment and are thus of interest to regulatory agencies and the general public. Multiple PFAS have been identified as potential endocrine-disrupting chemicals [1] due to estrogen receptor activation [2][3][4], impacts on puberty timing [5][6][7][8]. In this study, the uterotrophic assay was used to address the impact of PFAS as a mammalian endocrine disruptor. The uterotrophic assay is one of hundreds of OECD guideline tests that have been developed to test the potential hazard of chemicals. These guideline tests are internationally recognized and used by government, industry, and independent labs to identify potentially hazardous chemicals. The OECD guideline 440 uterotrophic assay is also used by the US EPA in its Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program. The uterotrophic assay and other guideline tests are used within regulatory science as steps needed for chemical product notification and registration. Previous work in other labs identified PFAS with estrogenic activation in fish or estrogen receptor activation with in vitro screens. Villeneuve et al. [7] used tiered testing, starting with in vitro estrogen receptor screening and further testing in fish for the estrogen sensitive endpoint of vitellogenin activation.
</snippet>

Title: Lessons learned, challenges, and opportunities: the U.S. Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program.
Snippet: Jeffrey P. Davis, Leah Zorrilla, Carolyn Favaro, Kelli Davis, Susan Borghoff Integrated Laboratory Systems, Inc., Research Triangle Park, NC 27709 The U.S. EPA Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) includes four in vivo mammalian assays to screen test substances for potential disruption of the estrogen, androgen, or thyroid hormone pathways. The Female Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function Assay (OPPTS 890.1450) screen for disruption of the estrogen, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, and thyroid hormone pathways. This assay is conducted in the female Sprague Dawley rat with daily test substance administration from postnatal (PND) 22 to 42/43. Daily body weights, clinical observations, and the day of vaginal opening and estrous cyclicity were evaluated. Two hours after the final dose administration, animals are humanely euthanized and blood and tissues are collected. Changes in tissue weights, serum hormone concentrations (thyroxine and thyroid stimulating hormone) and clinical chemistry endpoints, and histopathological evaluation of selected tissues (thyroid, ovaries, uterus, kidney) were evaluated. Here we demonstrate our ability to meet the performance criteria set forth by the test guidelines for data collected; including final body weight, day age and body weight at vaginal opening, tissue weights (liver, kidneys, adrenal glands, pituitary, ovaries, thyroid, and wet and blotted uterus), and thyroxine and thyroid stimulating hormone levels concentrations from multiple vehicles. We demonstrate that the performance criteria in the female pubertal assay are attainable and repeatable in our laboratory, and multiple vehicles may be used to administer the test substance without concern of meeting the performance criteria. The U.S. EPA Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) includes four in vivo mammalian assays to screen test substances for potential disruption of the estrogen, androgen, or thyroid hormone pathways. The Male Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function Assay (OPPTS 890.1500) screen for disruption of the androgen and thyroid hormone pathways, and hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
</snippet>

Title: Evaluating H295R steroidogenesis assay data for robust interpretation.
Snippet: Recently, a high-throughput adaptation of the H295R assay, measuring hormones and intermediates, was developed as a screening tool as part of the ToxCast program (Karmaus et al., 2016) that can provide insight into chemical effects and prioritize any additional testing if necessary (Haggard et al., 2018(Haggard et al., , 2019)). 

The use of the H295R assay in testing for putative endocrine disruptors has been recognized internationally; both the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) have developed test guidelines for using this assay to detect potential chemical perturbation of E2 and T production (Test guideline OCSPP 890.1550 (EPA, 2009a;2011b;Hecker et al., 2011;OECD Test Guideline 456 (OECD, 2011a)). The H295R steroidogenesis assay is also one of several Level 2 (in vitro) assays identified in the OECD Conceptual Framework for Testing and Assessment of Endocrine Disruptors and Guidance Document 150 (OECD, 2018a) as providing information on endocrine mechanisms. 

Criteria and guidance for identifying endocrine disruptors have been in force in Europe since November 2018 for all plant protection products (PPP) submissions (new or renewals) (ECHA/EFSA Guidance, Andersson et al., 2018) and European regulatory agencies are now regularly requesting the conduct of Level 2 in vitro assays to determine the endocrine activity of PPPs. The guidance reviews the estrogenic, androgenic, steroidogenic, and thyroid modalities, describes a minimum data set to be considered sufficiently investigated, and recommends a stepwise approach to testing.
</snippet>

Title: PFAS Modulate Osmotic Signaling Independent of Gravimetric Changes in the Rat Uterus
Snippet: The findings here report the results of the ovariectomized uterotrophic assay in adult rats that were orally exposed to a panel of PFAS at single-dose levels. The PFAS that were screened in the current assay included PFNA, PFHxS, PFOS, FC10-diol, FC8-diol, 8:2 FTOH, 6:2 FTOH, 4:2 FTOH, Nafion Byproduct2, and PFOSA. The PFAS used in this study were chosen based on previous estrogenic or hormonal activity in vitro [2], with hormonal sensitive endpoints in fish (activation of vitellogenic or estrogen-responsive genes a) [7,8] or with changes in puberty onset [5]. Previously published work with low doses of PFOA demonstrated increased wet uterine wet at only one dose with the immature rat uterotrophic assay [22], a different version of the uterotrophic assay which screens chemicals in young pre-pubertal animals. This study used the adult ovariectomized uterotrophic assay. Even though chemicals have been shown to induce estrogen-sensitive pathways in fish or with in vitro or receptor-mediated assays, the PFAS screened here did not induce significant uterine weight or fluid changes in the adult ovariectomized uterotrophic assay. The uterotrophic assay was developed as part of the standard guideline testing at the EPA under the Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (OCSPP Guideline 890.1600). These findings can be useful for the validation and assessment of endocrine disrupting screenings and methods spanning in vitro to in vivo extrapolation [23]. 

To build mechanistic understanding of PFAS-dependent changes in the uterus, osmotic gene arrays were used and compared to the estrogens. Osmotic array data were used to generate a heatmap and were also processed through ingenuity pathway analysis to show what pathways might be involved in PFAS signaling.
</snippet>

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of animal testing for endocrine disruption (ED), what has been done historically, how use has evolved, where it is still conducted today, and current trends toward replacement.

Summary
Historically, endocrine disruption testing relied on tiered in vivo batteries across mammals, fish, and amphibians to probe estrogen, androgen, thyroid, and steroidogenic modes of action, with U.S. EPA OPPTS and OECD guidelines formalizing these assays for regulatory use. Over the past decade, jurisdictions (notably the EU and UK) have substantially reduced animal testing for cosmetics and have increasingly embraced OECD-aligned in vitro/in silico methods and weight-of-evidence approaches for endocrine endpoints; however, animal testing remains required or used in pesticide/bicide assessments and for certain rodent reproductive/thyroid screens where regulatory frameworks still demand conclusive adversity evidence. <cite id="73028920-0">Fish-focused OECD TGs (229, 230, 234, 240) and rodent OECD TGs (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) cover estrogen/androgen/steroidogenesis modalities, with amphibian TGs (231, 241, 248) for thyroid disruption; fish assays have become the primary non-mammalian vertebrate approach in environmental ED assessment</cite><cite id="73028920-1">Amphibian metamorphosis assay (OECD TG 231), larval growth/development (241), and Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid assay (248) are standardized in vivo options for thyroid-related endocrine disruption, whereas mammalian ED assessment relies on rodent assays such as TGs 407, 408, 416, 421, 422, and 443</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-2">OECD Guidance Document 150 and OPPTS guidelines provide a conceptual framework and standardized test descriptions for EATS pathways and are the basis for international data acceptance in regulatory assessments of endocrine disruption</cite>.

What animal tests have been done (historical and cross-jurisdiction)
Mammalian in vivo batteries (rodent reproductive and thyroid screens)
- In the U.S., the EPA Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) historically used four in vivo rodent assays spanning estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways: Female Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function (OPPTS 890.1450) and Male Pubertal Development and Thyroid Function (OPPTS 890.1500), with endpoint suites including vaginal opening, estrous cyclicity, tissue weights, serum hormones (thyroxine, TSH), and histopathology; these assays were designed to detect disruption of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal and thyroid axes in rats, and are part of the legacy OPPTS framework that informed OECD test design and acceptance. <cite id="3e35f408-1">The EDSP includes four in vivo mammalian assays screening estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways via rat pubertal development and thyroid function endpoints, with performance criteria demonstrably attainable and repeatable across labs</cite>.
- Estrogen/androgen receptor uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style screens and related rodent assays (e.g., OECD TG 443 rat uterotrophic assay; OECD TG 416 for androgen receptor activity in males) have long been used, often paired with fish-based vitellogenin screens to increase throughput while preserving biological plausibility. <cite id="3e35f408-0">The OECD 440 uterotrophic assay is used by the U.S. EPA EDSP; tiered approaches have combined in vitro receptor screening with fish vitellogenin assays to detect estrogen-sensitive endocrine effects</cite><cite id="3e35f408-3">The uterotrophic assay was developed under EPA EDSP (OCSPP 890.1600) and used in adult or immature rodent formats to detect estrogen-sensitive uterine responses</cite>.
- Steroidogenesis assays using H295R human adrenal cells are now widely recognized by OECD (TG 456) and EPA EDSP as Level 2 in vitro screens to detect perturbation of estrogen and testosterone production, and are integrated within OECD 150’s stepwise framework to reduce or replace animal testing when sufficient mechanistic and WOE data are available. <cite id="3e35f408-2">OECD TG 456 and EPA EDSP guideline 890.1550 recognize the H295R steroidogenesis assay; OECD 150 identifies Level 2 in vitro assays, including H295R, as mechanistic tools to determine endocrine activity and prioritize further testing</cite>.

Non-mammalian vertebrate in vivo assays (fish and amphibian)
- Fish assays historically and currently serve as core ED screening and tiered endpoints for environmental chemicals. OECD TG 229 (short-term fish reproduction), TG 230 (21-day fish screening), TG 234 (fish sexual development), and TG 240 (Medaka extended one-generation reproduction) provide standardized designs to detect estrogen-, androgen-, steroidogenesis-related, and thyroid-related disruption in fish, with increasing inclusion of thyroid endpoints in recent years. <cite id="73028920-0">OECD TGs 229, 230, 234, and 240 cover estrogen/androgen/steroidogenesis endpoints in fish; zebrafish has been widely used in in vivo ED studies, though thyroid-specific guidance historically lagged</cite>.
- Amphibian assays (metamorphosis, larval growth/development, and Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid) are standardized OECD TGs (231, 241, 248) and are recommended for thyroid-mode investigations in non-mammalian taxa, offering higher-tier biological relevance when exposure warrants. <cite id="73028920-1">Standardized amphibian assays (231, 241, 248) are recommended for investigating endocrine activity via the thyroid modality in non-mammalian vertebrates due to the amphibian TH axis control of metamorphosis</cite>.
- In pesticide/biocide contexts, EU/EFSA/ECHA frameworks have promoted tiered fish assays for ecological hazard identification and recommended amphibian assays for thyroid modes when needed; this reflects a shift toward aquatic vertebrates for environmental ED screening while retaining rodent assays for human-relevant endpoints. <cite id="73028920-0">EU projects have optimized aquatic vertebrate tests and moved to include thyroid endpoints in fish guidelines to reduce reliance on amphibians, with EATS modalities covered across TGs</cite><cite id="73028920-3">OECD’s conceptual framework and Level 3–5 tests (e.g., TG 229, 230, 231) are used in EU data requirements for PPP; EFSA’s tiered guidance emphasizes in vivo mammalian and fish assays for diverse hormonal functions, with amphibians prioritized at higher tiers if exposure concerns arise</cite><cite id="73028920-4">A tiered approach integrating exposure with hazard characterization recommends in vivo mammalian and fish assays for screening across estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways, with amphibians considered at higher tiers depending on exposure; avian and invertebrate tests can follow for reproductive and endocrine-mediated effects</cite>.

Cosmetics sector: large-scale decline and replacement
- The EU phased in a full ban on animal testing and sale of animal-tested cosmetics between 2004 (finished products) and 2009–2013 (ingredients), precipitating major reductions in cosmetic mammalian ED testing and parallel adoption of OECD in vitro methods for skin/eye irritation and acceptance of alternatives; similar bans or phase-outs have since been adopted in the UK, Turkey, Taiwan, New Zealand, and others. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">The UK first banned cosmetic animal testing in 1998; the EU implemented phased bans culminating in 2013, following which India adopted a 2014 ban and accepted OECD in vitro skin and eye irritation methods</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU legislation adopted scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors in 2017, effective for PPP/biocides in 2018, reinforcing a shift to alternative models and ethical strategies for endocrine assessment</cite>.
- EU-wide counts show mammalian ingredient testing peaked at 5,571 animals in 2005 and dropped to 1,245 by 2008, with the decline attributed to the ban’s first stages; these counts explicitly exclude ecotoxicity (fish LC50), reflecting regulatory movement away from mammalian toxicity for cosmetics. <cite id="bc9ecaed-4">Between 2004 and 2009 EU data show 5,571 mammalian toxicity animals in 2005 and 1,245 in 2008 for cosmetic ingredients, after the EU banned finished product testing in 2004 and ingredient testing phases in 2009; the full ban was completed in 2013</cite>.

How regulatory frameworks evolved and what they require now
- OECD Guidance Document 150 and OPPTS guidelines formalize a Conceptual Framework (levels 1–5) across biological organization to evaluate endocrine activity/adversity and to integrate in vitro, in silico, and in vivo evidence; this framework underpins mutual acceptance of data and has been adopted by EU biocide and PPP regulations. <cite id="bc9ecaed-2">OECD 150 provides guidance on interpreting test outcomes, tabulating endpoints and affected pathways, and using a Conceptual Framework for Testing and Assessment of Endocrine Disruptors to organize methods and determine additional testing needs; OECD/OPPTS methods are the basis for data acceptance in regulatory assessments</cite>.
- In the EU and ECHA/EFSA guidance for pesticides, in vivo fish assays (TG 229, 230, 234, 240) are primary for environmental ED screening, with amphibian assays recommended for thyroid modes and mammalian rodent assays still used for human-relevant endocrine adversity; integrated approaches and Level 2 in vitro assays (e.g., H295R, yeast estrogen screens) are encouraged to reduce animal use where sufficient evidence exists. <cite id="73028920-0">Testing across EATS modalities is covered by standardized TGs; fish have become the prime vertebrate class for ED assessment in the environment</cite><cite id="73028920-1">Amphibian assays (231, 241, 248) are recommended for thyroid-related ED investigation in non-mammalian species; rodent assays (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) underpin human assessment</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R steroidogenesis assays (OECD 456; EPA 890.1550) are recognized Level 2 in vitro methods that inform endocrine activity and prioritize further testing</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU data requirements have historically not been designed specifically for ED identification; OECD framework-level 3–5 tests (e.g., TG 229, 230, 231) are now included, with fish and amphibian assays prioritized for screening and higher-tier characterization</cite>.
- The EU has moved to adopt scientific criteria for endocrine disruption (effective for PPPs in 2018) and has incorporated OECD acceptance of in vitro test methods and Good In Vitro Method Practices, signaling a regulatory preference for integrated approaches that can de-incriminate or avoid animal tests when robust mechanistic and exposure evidence is available. <cite id="bc9ecaed-1">Scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors adopted by the EU in 2017/2018 align with WHO definitions and require datasets to assess disruptive capacity, encouraging alternative models when animal testing is not necessary</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD published guidance on defined approaches and accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes, and developed Good In Vitro Method Practices to extend GLP to in vitro methods</cite>.

Are these tests still being done today?
- Cosmetics and personal care: Following the EU’s completed ban (2013) and UK’s earlier ban (1998), and subsequent bans/phase-outs in multiple countries, animal testing for endocrine endpoints in cosmetics has been substantially reduced or eliminated; however, animal use persisted for ingredient testing until the phased implementation and is now being replaced by OECD-accepted in vitro methods in OECD-aligned jurisdictions. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">UK (1998) and EU (2013) bans led to adoption of OECD in vitro irritation/corrosion methods and harmonization of bans in India (2014)</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-4">EU ingredient mammalian testing fell from 5,571 in 2005 to 1,245 in 2008 before and during the first stage of the ban (2009), with the full ban completed by 2013</cite>.
- Plant protection products and biocides: EU and other regulators still require in vivo fish and amphibian assays for ED screening and characterization in environmental risk assessments; rodent assays remain the reference for human-relevant endocrine adversity, and Level 2 in vitro assays are increasingly requested to reduce animal numbers while providing mechanistic evidence. <cite id="73028920-0">EU projects optimize aquatic vertebrate tests and include thyroid endpoints in fish TGs to reduce amphibian reliance; fish assays (TG 229, 230, 234, 240) are central for ED identification in the environment</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide data requirements now incorporate OECD framework tests (229, 230, 231), with fish and amphibian assays prioritized for screening and higher-tier characterization</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">Regulatory agencies regularly request Level 2 in vitro assays (e.g., H295R) to determine endocrine activity of PPPs under OECD 150</cite>.
- Human health endpoints in general chemicals: U.S. EPA EDSP continues to use in vivo rodent assays for conclusive adversity assessment, alongside tiered in vitro approaches; OECD TGs (e.g., 440/443) and OPPTS protocols remain in use, but agencies increasingly accept Tox21-style in vitro/IT strategies to waive some animal tests when evidence is sufficient. <cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s in vivo rodent assays for estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways (e.g., OPPTS 890.1450/1500) remain standardized</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA’s collaboration with Tox21 enabled waivers of animal-based uterotrophic testing, marking the first regulatory use of this approach to replace animal testing</cite>.
- Research and surveillance: Scientists continue to run classic rodent uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style and fish vitellogenin assays to detect estrogenicity in emerging compounds (e.g., PFAS), reflecting ongoing use of established assays even as alternatives proliferate. <cite id="3e35f408-0">PFAS have been screened for estrogen receptor activation and endocrine disruption using uterotrophic assays (OECD 440/EDSP), with tiered strategies pairing in vitro receptor screening and fish vitellogenin assays</cite><cite id="3e35f408-3">Adult and immature rat uterotrophic formats detect estrogen-sensitive uterine responses and remain a standard in regulatory-guided screening</cite>.

What has replaced animal tests and how accepted are alternatives?
- In vitro mechanistic assays and integrated approaches: The H295R steroidogenesis assay (OECD 456; EPA 890.1550), yeast estrogen screen (YES), and other Level 2 methods are recognized by OECD/EPA to detect pathway-level disruption and reduce or replace animal testing when combined with computational models and weight-of-evidence reasoning. <cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R steroidogenesis assays are recognized by OECD and EPA to detect perturbation of estrogen and testosterone production and are used within OECD 150 to prioritize additional testing or conclude endocrine activity</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">Alternative models are required to assess endocrine safety for cosmetics ethically; OECD 150 describes how adversity can be assessed using validated in vitro/embryonic models to cover EATS pathways without animal experimentation when justified</cite>.
- Institutional acceptance and Good Practice: OECD has accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes and formalized Good In Vitro Method Practices (GIVIMP), enabling broader acceptance of in vitro ED assays in regulatory dossiers. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD accepted ecotoxicity tests based on fish cell lines and rainbow trout hepatocytes and published Good In Vitro Method Practices to extend GLP to in vitro methods</cite>.
- Weight-of-evidence and regulatory WOs: Multiple jurisdictions now implement integrated approaches to testing and assessment (IATA), encouraging combinations of defined approaches (e.g., in vitro receptor assays, H295R, QSAR) to de-incriminate or avoid animal tests when data gaps are small and exposure is low; EU legislation explicitly adopts scientific criteria to define ED properties and aligns with OECD frameworks. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD published guidance on defined approaches and reporting within integrated testing strategies</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU adopted scientific criteria for endocrine disruptors in 2017/2018 aligned with WHO definitions and supports the use of alternative models and ethical strategies for endocrine assessment</cite>.

Putting it together: historical practices and current status
- What was done: Endocrine disruption testing historically relied on in vivo mammalian rodent reproductive/developmental assays (estrogen, androgen, thyroid) and non-mammalian vertebrate assays in fish and amphibians to probe EATS modalities; these were standardized by U.S. OPPTS and OECD and implemented across pesticides, biocides, and cosmetics. <cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s rodent pubertal and thyroid function assays provided standardized screens for hormonal disruption</cite><cite id="73028920-0">OECD TGs 229, 230, 234, and 240 cover fish EATS endpoints; amphibian TGs (231, 241, 248) target thyroid disruption; rodent TGs (407, 408, 416, 421, 422, 443) underpin human assessment</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide guidance incorporated OECD framework and fish/amphibian assays to identify ED properties in non-target organisms</cite>.
- Are they still done? Today, in vivo ED assays remain required or frequently used for environmental hazard identification (fish and amphibian assays) and for human-relevant adversity in regulatory frameworks, especially for PPPs and biocides; rodent uterotrophic/vaginal cytology-style and other in vivo assays are still run by EPA and researchers, but OECD/EPA frameworks now enable waivers or replacement in many cases via Tox21-style strategies and recognized in vitro assays. <cite id="73028920-0">Fish assays are the prime vertebrate class for ED assessment in the environment, with amphibians covering thyroid modes</cite><cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP continues to use four in vivo rodent assays for mammalian ED screening</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA’s Tox21 collaboration enabled waivers of animal uterotrophic testing, marking the first regulatory use of this approach</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD accepted fish cell-line ecotoxicity tests and established GIVIMP, supporting broader acceptance of in vitro methods</cite>.
- Sectoral trends: Cosmetics testing in OECD-aligned jurisdictions has been largely halted or replaced by in vitro methods following EU/UK bans, with counts of mammalian ingredient tests dropping precipitously in the EU before and after the phased ban; in contrast, pesticide/biocide and broader chemical safety assessments still rely on in vivo assays but increasingly integrate OECD-accepted in vitro tools and weight-of-evidence to minimize animal use. <cite id="bc9ecaed-3">EU/UK bans and adoption of OECD in vitro methods catalyzed large-scale replacement of cosmetic animal tests</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-4">EU ingredient mammalian testing fell from 5,571 to 1,245 animals between 2005 and 2008 as the first stage of the ban took effect (full ban by 2013)</cite><cite id="73028920-3">EU pesticide guidance incorporates OECD TGs for fish and amphibian assays and emphasizes integrated approaches</cite>.

What to expect next
Regulators and industry are moving toward routine use of defined approaches and integrated testing strategies, with OECD and EFSA/ECHA explicitly endorsing in vitro, in silico, and GLP-extended methods; this trajectory implies further reductions in animal testing for endocrine endpoints where mechanistic and exposure data are strong, with in vivo studies reserved for cases requiring conclusive adversity evidence or where alternatives are insufficient. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">OECD’s defined approaches reporting guidance and acceptance of fish cell-line ecotoxicity tests, along with GIVIMP, support broader adoption of in vitro methods</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU criteria define endocrine disruption via mode of action, adverse effect, and plausibility, encouraging datasets that leverage in vitro/embryonic models to avoid animal experimentation when feasible</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">Recognition of H295R and other Level 2 assays within OECD 150 enables regulatory determinations of endocrine activity and prioritization of additional testing, reducing reliance on animals where evidence suffices</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- Yes, many of the classic in vivo animal tests for endocrine disruption have long been used and are still used in certain jurisdictions and sectors—especially for environmental hazard identification (fish, amphibian) and human-relevant adversity (rodent reproductive/thyroid screens). <cite id="73028920-0">Fish and amphibian assays remain core to environmental ED testing, with rodent assays for human adversity</cite><cite id="3e35f408-1">EDSP’s rodent assays continue as standardized screens</cite>.
- No, they are not universally “still” required: OECD/EU/US frameworks increasingly accept and mandate the use of in vitro, in silico, and integrated approaches to replace or reduce animal testing for endocrine endpoints, with cosmetics largely off the animal-testing track in many jurisdictions and tiered strategies (e.g., Tox21) enabling waivers in some mammalian assays. <cite id="bc9ecaed-0">EPA has used Tox21 to waive animal uterotrophic tests; OECD accepts fish cell-line ecotoxicity and formalizes GIVIMP</cite><cite id="bc9ecaed-1">EU criteria and OECD 150 encourage alternative models and integrated approaches to avoid animal testing when sufficient evidence exists</cite>.
- What to watch: Continued OECD/EU acceptance of in vitro ED assays (e.g., H295R, yeast estrogen screens) and growth of integrated approaches will likely further de-incriminate animal tests for endocrine disruption in human health risk assessments, while in vivo fish/amphibian assays will remain pivotal for environmental risk characterization where full biological and exposure context is required. <cite id="73028920-0">EU efforts to include thyroid endpoints in fish TGs aim to reduce amphibian reliance while covering EATS modalities in non-mammalian vertebrates</cite><cite id="3e35f408-2">H295R and other Level 2 assays provide mechanistic evidence and support regulatory decisions to minimize animal testing</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Development of the integrated fish endocrine disruptor test—Part B: Implementation of thyroid‐related endpoints
Snippet: Various ongoing European Union (EU) research projects are working on the optimization of aquatic vertebrate tests for the identification of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs; Holbech et al., 2020).Attempts are being made to cover as many relevant modes of action as possible, to include thyroid-related endpoints in existing fish test guidelines (TGs) and thus, to reduce existing amphibian tests.Testing for the different endocrine modalities (EATS: estrogen, androgen, thyroid, and steroidogenesis) is covered in different TGs for nontarget organisms (ECHA/EFSA, 2018).For nonmammalian vertebrates, tests covering endpoints for estrogen-, androgen-, and steroidogenesis-related effects in fish are covered by TGs 229 (Fish Short-Term Reproduction Assay [FSTRA]; OECD, 2012), 230 (21-Day Fish Assay;OECD, 2009b), 234 (Fish Sexual Development Test [FSDT]; OECD, 2011), and 240 (Medaka Extended One Generation Reproduction Test; OECD, 2023).Fish have thus become the prime vertebrate class for the assessment of EDCs in the environment.

However, although zebrafish (Danio rerio) has been the major nonmammalian model utilized in studies evaluating in vivo effects on the TH system or discussing regulatory concerns over the past five years (Couderq et al., 2020), none of these TGs addresses potential TH system disruption (THSD).So far, in an environmental context, thyroid-related endocrine disruption is covered only for amphibians by three OECD TGs (TGs 231, 241, and 248;OECD, 2009a), and assessment of THSD for humans is based mainly on rodent assays such as TGs 407, 408, 416, 421, 422, and 443 (ECHA/EFSA, 2018).

Title: Amphibian studies to investigate the endocrine-disrupting properties of chemicals through the thyroid modality: a comparison of their statistical power
Snippet: Regulation 2018/605 (European Commission, 2018) lays down the scientific criteria for the identification of pesticide active substances having endocrine-disrupting (ED) properties. To support the implementation of those criteria, a guidance document was jointly developed by the European Chemical Agency (ECHA) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) with the participation of the Joint Research Centre (ECHA/EFSA, 2018). In accordance with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) guidance document on standardised test guidelines for evaluating chemicals for endocrine disruption (OECD, 2018), the ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends using amphibian studies for investigating the ED properties in nonmammalian species through the Thyroid-(T) modality, because it is well established that amphibian metamorphosis is under the control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. In case of uncertainties around some of the definitions used in this study, for example, "endocrine activity," "endocrine adversity," "sufficiently investigate," "T-modality," "T-mediated," "positive findings," "screening assay," and so forth, please refer to the ECHA/EFSA Guidance (2018) for clarification. Two standardized in vivo amphibian study designs are available to sufficiently investigate the endocrine activity and/or adversity of plant protection products through the T-modality. These studies are the amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA, OECD test guideline 231, OECD, 2009; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency [USEPA], 2009) and the larval amphibian growth and developmental assay (LADGA, OECD test guideline 241, OECD, 2015;USEPA, 2015). A third assay, the Xenopus eleutheroembryonic thyroid assay (XETA, OECD test guideline 248, OECD, 2019) is also available. However, the XETA is only aimed at detecting thyroid active compounds based on induction of fluorescence compared to controls (Arena & van der Linden, 2021).

Title: Computational Approaches to Chemical Hazard Assessment
Snippet: The OECD guideline identifier provides detailed descriptions of different experimental procedures. OECD TG 407, for example, is the OECD guideline for the test "Repeated Dose 28-Day Oral Toxicity Study in Rodents" (OECD, 2008). This is a 13-page guideline, which has a revision history (one major change in 1995) that covers important initial considerations, the principle of the test, and a detailed description of the method. These guidelines describe in some detail how to interpret the results of guideline studies and what parameters may be changed for the study. Parameter choices for TG 407 include selection of animal species (preferably rats, but any rodent with sufficient justification.) The ability to change parameter selection for guidelines allows greater experimental variance. OECD guideline outcomes make excellent QSAR targets. They are the result of a well-defined study with careful instructions on how to measure the results. However, even using results from OECD guidelines studies is not without peril. In a study of the consistency of the Draize rabbit eye irritation test (another OECD guideline study), we found a low rate of concordance between studies (Luechtefeld et al., 2016b). Variance in repeated guideline study results can be large and bias can exist between labs performing experiments.

Title: Guidance on tiered risk assessment for plant protection products for aquatic organisms in edge-of-field surface waters

Title: Ecological risk assessment of endocrine disruptors.
Snippet: The European Centre for Ecotoxicology and Toxicology of Chemicals proposes a tiered approach for the ecological risk assessment of endocrine disruptors, integrating exposure and hazard (effects) characterization. Exposure assessment for endocrine disruptors should direct specific tests for wildlife species, placing hazard data into a risk assessment context. Supplementing the suite of mammalian screens now under Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) validation, high priority should be given to developing a fish screening assay for detecting endocrine activity in oviparous species. Taking into account both exposure characterization and alerts from endocrine screening, higher tier tests are also a priority for defining adverse effects. We propose that in vivo mammalian and fish assays provide a comprehensive screening battery for diverse hormonal functions (including androgen, estrogen, and thyroid hormone), whereas Amphibia should be considered at higher tiers if there are exposure concerns. Higher tier endocrine-disruptor testing should include fish development and fish reproduction tests, whereas a full life-cycle test could be subsequently used to refine aquatic risk assessments when necessary. For avian risk assessment, the new OECD Japanese quail reproduction test guideline provides a valuable basis for developing a test to detecting endocrine-mediated reproductive effects; this species could be used, where necessary, for an avian life-cycle test. For aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, data from existing developmental and reproductive tests remain of high value for ecological risk assessment. High priority should be given to research into comparative endocrine physiology of invertebrates to support data extrapolation to this diverse fauna.
